ety.text: From Middle English whatever. By surface analysis, what + -ever.

senses.d: A thing or person whose actual name is unknown or forgotten.
ex: As far as I'm concerned Alec is dead. Whatever they've got in there, that...whatever.

senses.d: What ever; emphatic form of 'what'.
ex: Good heavens! Whatever time is it?!

senses.d: Regardless of the ... that; for any ... that.
ex: Whatever your choice, there will be consequences.
I will stick with you, whatever fate befalls us.

senses.d: Any ... that; of no matter what type or kind that.
ex: Whatever doubts I had were quickly dispelled.
Write down whatever thoughts come into your mind.

senses.d: Any; of no matter what type or kind.
ex: He must be stopped, whatever the cost.

senses.d: What ever; emphasised form of 'what', used to ask which thing, event, circumstance, etc.
ex: Whatever do you mean?

Whatever happened to Leon Trotsky?
He got an ice pick
That made his ears burn

senses.d: Regardless of anything that.
ex: Whatever he does, he will still lose the game.
Whatever happens, stay calm.

senses.d: Anything that; all that.
ex: Do whatever works.
I’ll do whatever I can.

senses.d: Anything; thing(s) of unspecified kind, or no matter what kind; sometimes used to indicate that the speaker does not care about options.
ex: I don't need any of this stuff, so take whatever.
"As far as I'm concerned, Alec is dead. Whatever they've got in there, that — whatever —."

senses.d: At all; in any way; whatsoever.
ex: There is no point whatever in going on with this discussion.
He is quite unconscious; and, though your presence is a relief to me, you must remember that there is no hope - no hope whatever.

senses.d: In what way; to what extent.
ex: Whatever does it matter now?

senses.d: A holophrastic expression used to dismiss something that the speaker doesn't care about, doesn't think important, or doesn't want to consider or discuss any further. Sometimes conceived as an ellipsis of whatever you say, implying feigned deference: whatever you say [apparently must be true].
ex: Near-synonyms: meh, so what
So you broke it? Whatever! Get a grip.

senses.d: Unexceptional or unimportant; blah.
ex: All in all, I guess I shouldn't be complaining, but the rest of the show, imho, was very whatever-ish.
She's like so whatever / You can do so much better

senses.d: Something whose exact kind or nature is unimportant; a thingy.

grp.label: regardless of the … that; for any … that
indicating the speaker does not care what someone says

ety.text: Literally, “any thing”.

fr:bof.gl: so what, never mind, whatever, meh

fr:qu'importe.gl: whichever you like, it doesn't matter, no matter, whatever

ety.text: From Middle English what, from Old English hwæt (“what”), from Proto-West Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Germanic *hwat (“what”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷód (“what”), neuter form of *kʷós (“who”). Cognate with Scots what, whit (“what”), North Frisian wat (“what”), Saterland Frisian wat (“what”), West Frisian wat (“what”), Dutch wat (“what”), Low German wat (“what”), German was (“what”), Danish hvad (“what”), Norwegian Bokmål hva (“what”), Swedish vad (“what”), Norwegian Nynorsk kva (“what”), Icelandic hvað (“what”), Latin quod (“what, which”).

senses.d: Which, especially which of an open-ended set of possibilities.
ex: What colour are you going to use?
What time is it?

senses.d: Which.
ex: I wonder what colour he is going to use.
I know what colour I am going to use.

senses.d: Any ... that; all ... that; whatever.
ex: He seems to have lost what sense he had.
What money I earn is soon spent.

senses.d: Emphasises that something is noteworthy or remarkable in quality or degree, in either a good or bad way; may be used in combination with certain other determiners, especially 'a', less often 'some'.
ex: This shows what beauty there is in nature.
You know what nonsense she talks.

senses.d: Used to form exclamations indicating that something is remarkable, in either a good or bad way.
ex: What nonsense!
Wow! What a speech.

senses.d: Which thing, event, circumstance, etc.: used in asking for the specification of an identity, quantity, quality, etc.
ex: Hammer in that nail —What with? I didn't bring my set of tools.
What is your name?

senses.d: That which; those that; the thing(s) that.
ex: He knows what he wants and what to do to get it.
What is amazing is his boundless energy.

senses.d: Anything that; all that; whatever.
ex: I will do what I can to help you.
What I'll do is, I'll phone you to let you know.

senses.d: That; which; who.
ex: Look! It's that bloke again what was 'ere yesterday!
It's all to do with the crossing in the river[,] what we're gonna get to shortly. … there's a trust what manages it for the king [..]

senses.d: In what way; to what extent.
ex: What does it matter?
What do you care?

senses.d: Used before a prepositional phrase to emphasise that something is taken into consideration as a cause or reason; usually used in combination with 'with' (see what with), and much less commonly with other prepositions.
An expression of surprise or disbelief.
ex: What! That’s amazing!
wait this song is so good whattt

senses.d: What do you want? An abrupt, usually unfriendly enquiry as to what a person desires.
ex: What? I'm busy.

senses.d: What did you say? I beg your pardon? This usage is often considered impolite, with the more polite "Pardon?" or "Excuse me?" preferred.
ex:
— Could I have some of those aarrrrrr mmmm ...
— What?

senses.d: Indicating a guess or approximation, or a pause to try to recall information.
ex: I must have been, what, about five years old.

senses.d: Something; thing; stuff.
The identity of a thing, as an answer to a question of what.
ex: The emphasis on the interplay between the hows and whats of interpretive practice is paramount.

senses.d: Something that is addressed by what, as opposed to a person, addressed by who.
ex:
2012, "We Are Both", season 2, episode 2 of Once Upon a Time
Regina: What are you?
Rumplestiltskin: What? What? What? My, my, what a rude question! I am not a what.

senses.d: Emphasizes the truth of an assertion made to contradict an evidently false assumption held by the listener.
ex: Pitch contour: low [wʌt˩], low-dipping [wʌt˨˩]

— Sian sia, nearby here don’t have library.
— The National Library is a five-minute walk from here what, no meh?

senses.d: Used to invite agreement or acknowledgment when something is assumed to be straightforward or already obvious to begin with; similar in function to “right?” and “as you know”.
ex: Pitch contour: low [wʌt˩], low-dipping [wʌt˨˩]
If it doesn’t get sunlight, it won’t grow what, so you should consider moving it closer to the window.

senses.d: Used after a direct assertion to reinforce a disagreeing opinion.
ex: Pitch contour: low [wʌt˩], low-dipping [wʌt˨˩]
The lava cakes are not that bad what.

From Latin quid; ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷid, compare *kʷís. Cognate to English what, which differs due to changing under Grimm’s law.

fr:qu'est-ce que.gl: what, what is it that (used as an interrogative for a direct object)

ety.text: Literally, “what is this that”.
Inherited from Latin causa. Doublet of the borrowing causa. The pronoun is a clipping of che cosa.

ety.text: From Middle English whal, whale, from Old English hwæl (“whale”), from Proto-West Germanic *hwal, from Proto-Germanic *hwalaz (“whale”) (compare German Wal, Swedish val, Danish and Norwegian Bokmål hval, Norwegian Nynorsk kval; compare also Dutch walvis, West Frisian walfisk, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kʷálos (“sheatfish”) (compare German Wels, Latin squalus (“big sea fish”), Old Prussian kalis, Ancient Greek ἄσπαλος (áspalos), Avestan 𐬐𐬀𐬭𐬀 (kara, “kind of fish”)).
Uncertain. Perhaps a variant of wale influenced by whack, whap, etc.

senses.d: Any large cetacean, usually with the exclusion of dolphins and porpoises.
ex: Near-synonym: baleen (obsolete sense)

senses.d: Any species of Cetacea, including dolphins and porpoises.
Something, or someone, that is very large.
ex: It was a whale of a job. […] It took two months, and the fair blush of youth off my cheeks.

senses.d: Something, or someone, that is excellent.
ex: They were having a whale of a time when a very stern looking shop assistant came over to tell them off.

senses.d: A gambler who routinely wagers large amounts of money.
ex: These are often no-limit games as maximum bets cramp a whale’s style.

senses.d: An investor who deals with very large amounts of money.
A person who spends large amounts of money on things that are marketed to them.
ex: Whales are the big spenders who drop huge amounts of money into a game.

senses.d: An overweight person (usually a woman)
ex: The whale is still snoring. He's a real beauty, the whale. Got this thick curly hair all over his chest and stomach and legs.

senses.d: To hunt for whales.
To thrash, to flog, to beat vigorously or soundly.
ex: Brought him back, put him in the stall—low stable—got out of his reach, and then begun to whale him. Then he kicked up agin; […]
For quotations using this term, see Citations:whale.

senses.d: An artificial landing place for ships on a riverbank or shore.
ex: Commerce pushes its wharves into the sea.
Out upon the wharfs they came, / Knight and burgher, lord and dame, / And round the prow they read her name, / The Lady of Shalott.

senses.d: Any bank of a river or shore of a sea.
ex: the fat weed that roots itself in ease on Lethe wharf

senses.d: To secure by a wharf.
To place on a wharf.
